title: Activity & Fragment Lifecycle
summary: The exact Android callback sequence, why a rotation destroys and recreates your Activity, and where state should actually live to survive it.

slides.markdown:
The cross-platform [app lifecycle](app-lifecycle-process-model) model — active, background, suspended, killed — has a concrete Android implementation with named callbacks you get to override: `onCreate`, `onStart`, `onResume`, `onPause`, `onStop`, `onDestroy`. Every Android developer has to know this sequence cold, because it's where you correctly start and stop work tied to visibility.

The twist Android adds: a simple screen rotation **destroys and recreates your Activity** by default — the same teardown-and-rebuild path as a process death, just far more frequent and easier to hit by accident. This topic covers the exact callback order, why rotation triggers recreation, Fragment lifecycle layered on top, and how to actually survive both without losing state.

slides.sectionTitle: The Activity lifecycle callbacks in order
slides.markdown:
Six callbacks, in a fixed order for a normal launch: `onCreate` (Activity object created, views inflated, one-time setup) → `onStart` (Activity becoming visible) → `onResume` (Activity in the foreground, interactive — this is "active" in the cross-platform model). Going away reverses it: `onPause` (losing focus, but still visible — a dialog appeared over it) → `onStop` (no longer visible) → `onDestroy` (Activity object being torn down).

The pairs matter more than the individual names: `onStart`/`onStop` bracket visibility, `onResume`/`onPause` bracket interactivity. Work that only matters while visible (starting an animation, registering a listener) belongs in `onStart`/`onStop`; work that only matters while actively in the foreground (resuming a camera preview, acquiring a sensor) belongs in `onResume`/`onPause`. Starting something in `onCreate` that should really start in `onResume` is a common source of wasted work when the Activity is created but never actually becomes interactive right away.

The six callbacks form a state machine, not a strict one-way sequence — an Activity can loop between `onResume` and `onPause` many times (a dialog appears and dismisses repeatedly) without ever reaching `onStop`, and can go `onStop` → `onStart` → `onResume` (backgrounded, then foregrounded again) without a fresh `onCreate`, as long as the OS didn't destroy the process in between.

Only a full `onDestroy` followed by a fresh `onCreate` means the Activity object itself was recreated — everything else is the *same* Activity instance moving between visible/invisible and interactive/non-interactive, which is why in-memory fields survive a pause/resume cycle but not a destroy/recreate cycle.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a configuration change recreates your Activity
slides.markdown:
Rotating the device is a **configuration change** — the same category as switching language, entering split-screen, or changing dark mode. By default, Android's answer to any configuration change is blunt: destroy the current Activity entirely and create a brand new one with the new configuration applied, rather than trying to patch the existing instance in place.

The reasoning: many resources genuinely depend on configuration — a layout XML file has separate versions for portrait/landscape, a string resource can vary by locale — and rather than building a mechanism to selectively re-fetch just the resources that changed, Android tears down and rebuilds the whole Activity so it re-reads every configuration-dependent resource from scratch, guaranteeing correctness at the cost of doing real work on every rotation.

This means **every rotation is a `onDestroy` + `onCreate` cycle** by default — the same teardown your Activity would face from a process death, just happening far more often and far more predictably. Anything that doesn't survive that cycle will visibly reset on every rotation unless you've explicitly designed around it.

slides.sectionTitle: Fragment lifecycle layered on top of its host Activity
slides.markdown:
A Fragment has its own lifecycle callbacks — `onCreateView`, `onViewCreated`, `onDestroyView`, `onDestroy` — layered *inside* its host Activity's lifecycle, which adds real complexity: a Fragment's view can be destroyed and recreated (`onDestroyView`/`onCreateView`) independently of the Fragment object itself being destroyed, most commonly when the Fragment goes into the back stack but stays in memory.

This split matters because it's a frequent source of a specific bug class: holding a reference to a view in a field that outlives `onDestroyView` — the view is gone, but code still tries to touch it, either crashing or silently no-op-ing depending on the exact reference. The fix is nulling out view references in `onDestroyView`, not just in `onDestroy`, and never holding view state longer than the view itself is guaranteed to live.

A Fragment cannot outlive its host Activity — when the Activity is destroyed, every attached Fragment goes through its own teardown as part of that same cycle, in a well-defined nested order.

slides.sectionTitle: onSaveInstanceState vs ViewModel for surviving rotation
slides.markdown:
| | `onSaveInstanceState` (Bundle) | ViewModel |
|---|---|---|
| **Survives rotation** | Yes | Yes |
| **Survives process death** | Yes (Bundle is written to disk) | No — held only in memory |
| **Data size** | Small — meant for primitives/parcelables, not large objects | Any size, including live objects, network clients, in-flight state |
| **When to use** | Small UI state you need back even after a process death (scroll position, form field text) | Screen-level state and business logic you want to survive rotation without re-fetching, but that doesn't need to survive a full process kill |

The two aren't competitors — they solve different halves of the problem. `ViewModel` is retained across the Activity being destroyed and recreated *for a configuration change specifically* (Android keeps the same ViewModel instance alive through that recreation), which is why it survives rotation without needing to re-run a network call. It does **not** survive an actual process death, which is what `onSaveInstanceState`'s Bundle is for — small enough data that writing it to a Bundle that goes through the OS's own state-saving path is cheap and reliable.

slides.sectionTitle: Restoring UI state in onCreate from a saved Bundle
slides.markdown:
The Bundle passed into `onCreate` is non-null exactly when the Activity is being recreated from a previous saved state — a rotation, or a restoration after process death — and null on a genuinely fresh launch, which is the standard way to distinguish the two.

```kotlin
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

    val scrollPosition = savedInstanceState?.getInt("scroll_position") ?: 0
    recyclerView.scrollToPosition(scrollPosition)
}

override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    outState.putInt("scroll_position", recyclerView.firstVisiblePosition())
}
```

`onSaveInstanceState` is called before the Activity is destroyed whenever the system anticipates it might need to recreate it (not on every pause — the OS decides), so relying on it for anything time-critical or expecting it every single time you background is the wrong mental model; it's specifically for surviving configuration changes and OS-initiated recreation, not a general-purpose save hook.

slides.sectionTitle: Fragment transactions and the back stack
slides.markdown:
Swapping Fragments in and out of a container happens through a `FragmentTransaction` — add, remove, replace, optionally adding the transaction to the **back stack** so the system back gesture reverses it, returning to the previous Fragment rather than exiting the Activity.

A Fragment on the back stack but not currently displayed still exists as an object (its Fragment lifecycle survives), but its view is destroyed (`onDestroyView` has run) — this is exactly the split lifecycle covered above showing up in practice. Popping the back stack recreates the view via `onCreateView` again on the same Fragment instance, not a new one, which is why state held in the Fragment's own fields (not its view) survives a back-stack round trip cleanly, while anything held only in the view itself does not.

A common transaction mistake is committing a transaction after the Activity's state has already been saved (post `onSaveInstanceState`) — Android will throw or silently drop the transaction depending on which commit method is used, because the transaction's effect can no longer be reliably restored if the Activity gets recreated right after.

slides.sectionTitle: Leaking an Activity by holding its Context in a static field
slides.markdown:
A singleton or static helper caches a `Context` — often the Activity itself, passed in for convenience — in a static field so it doesn't have to be passed around everywhere. The Activity later gets destroyed (rotation, backgrounding, navigation away), but the static field still holds a reference to it, which means the garbage collector can never reclaim that Activity's entire object graph — every view, every bitmap, everything it was holding — for as long as the app process lives.

This is one of the most common Android-specific memory leaks precisely because it looks completely harmless — the code compiles, runs fine in a quick test, and the leak only becomes visible as a slow accumulation of dead Activities piling up in memory across many rotations or navigations, eventually showing up as an out-of-memory crash far removed in time from the actual bug.

The fix: never store an Activity Context in anything with a lifetime longer than the Activity itself. Use `applicationContext` for anything that genuinely needs to outlive the Activity (it has no attached UI state to leak), and prefer a `WeakReference` or an explicit lifecycle-aware callback registration/unregistration for anything that must hold an Activity-scoped reference temporarily.

slides.sectionTitle: Doing heavy work in onCreate and slowing cold start
slides.markdown:
`onCreate` is on the critical path to the first frame the user sees — anything synchronous and slow here (a large file read, a network call executed and awaited, heavy object graph construction) directly delays when the Activity becomes interactive, and it happens on **every** creation, including every rotation, not just the app's cold start.

This is easy to miss in development because a dev device with a fast SoC and warm caches makes a 200ms `onCreate` feel instant, while the same code on a lower-end device with cold disk caches can be several times slower — the exact device split that platform-level metrics tools attribute per app and that real users disproportionately experience on cheaper hardware.

The fix is deferring anything not needed for the first frame: kick off asynchronous work in `onCreate` rather than blocking on it, lazily initialize objects only when first actually used rather than eagerly in the constructor path, and specifically re-examine anything expensive that runs on *every* rotation, not just app launch, since a rotation-triggered `onCreate` re-runs the exact same code with no caching unless you've explicitly added it.
